title: Exercise 15.1: Limits of Algebraic Functions
notes: **Topic focus:** Finding limits of polynomial and rational functions.
**Polynomial limits:** For polynomial p(x), lim(x→a) p(x) = p(a) — simply substitute.
**Rational function limits:** For rational function p(x)/q(x), substitute if q(a) ≠ 0.
**Indeterminate forms:** If substitution gives 0/0, factor and simplify before evaluating.
**Common techniques:** Factoring, rationalization, dividing by highest power of x.
**Example type 2:** lim(x→∞) (3x²+2x)/(2x²-1) = 3/2 by dividing by x².
**Connection:** These techniques use the standard limits and algebraic manipulation.
**Practice source:** Exercise 15.1 from the textbook with detailed solutions available.
confusion: Direct substitution only works when the function is defined at the point — check for 0/0 first.
Don't forget to factor completely before canceling — partial factoring leads to errors.
For limits at infinity, divide by the highest power of x in the denominator.
Confusing lim(x→∞) with lim(x→a): the techniques are different for each case.
Don't apply L'Hôpital's rule here — use algebraic manipulation as intended at this level.
practice: Find lim(x→0) (√(1+x)-1)/x by rationalizing the numerator.
Evaluate lim(x→2) (x³-8)/(x-2) using difference of cubes factorization.
Find lim(x→∞) (5x²+3x-1)/(2x²-x+4) by dividing by highest power.
universalFacts: Polynomial functions are continuous everywhere, so direct substitution always works.
Rational functions are continuous except where the denominator equals zero.
The factorization technique works because (x-a) is a factor of p(x)-p(a).
Limits at infinity reveal horizontal asymptotes of rational functions.
These algebraic limit techniques form the foundation for understanding derivatives.
